analysis.one_liner: Requires ranked choice voting for all congressional elections and pays states to switch.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2025 with 16 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Democrats; it has sat in the House Administration Committee since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every state to use ranked choice voting in elections for the U.S. House and Senate — primaries, special elections, and general elections — starting with elections in 2030. Under ranked choice voting, voters rank candidates in order of preference, and the candidate with the fewest votes is dropped round by round, with those votes transferred to the next choice, until someone wins a majority. The bill bans separate runoff elections, sets uniform ballot and counting rules, and gives states federal money — $4 to $8 per registered voter — to upgrade voting equipment, train poll workers, and educate voters. Voters who believe a state is not following the rules could sue, with fast-track court procedures.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in congressional elections, particularly supporters of third-party and independent candidates who currently face pressure not to 'waste' their votes, since ranking lets people vote their true first choice without handing the race to their least favorite candidate. Winners must reach majority support rather than splitting the vote. States get federal money to cover the switch. Minor parties and independents gain because their candidates can be ranked without spoiling an election.

how_it_helps.text: Each state must run all congressional primaries, special elections, and general elections using ranked choice voting, and no state may hold a separate runoff election after the initial election date [S2].

Ballots must let voters rank at least five candidates (or all candidates if fewer), include all qualified candidates and write-in options to the extent state law allows, and carry instructions explaining how to rank [S2].

Ballots are counted in rounds: the lowest vote-getter is eliminated and those ballots transfer to each voter's next-ranked active candidate, until a candidate wins a majority; blank ballots and exhausted ballots drop out of the count [S2].

States that use open, nonpartisan primaries may keep them, but at least three candidates must advance to the general election, and party ballot-access vote counts are measured from whichever counting round gave the candidate the most votes — a rule that protects minor parties' ballot lines [S2].

By June 1, 2026, each state would receive a federal payment of $4 to $8 per registered voter to cover voting equipment updates, software, ballot printing, poll worker training, audits, and voter education about ranked choice voting [S2].

Any person living in a state that fails to follow the requirements could sue in federal court, with expedited three-judge-court review, attorney's fees available, and jurisdiction concentrated in D.C. or the state capital to speed cases [S2].
The bill states it does not affect elections for state and local offices, and it does not take effect until elections held on or after January 1, 2030, giving states years to adjust [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the state implementation grants, with an open-ended authorization of 'such sums as may be necessary.' Election administrators bear real work: reprogramming or replacing voting equipment, redesigning ballots, training poll workers, and educating voters, with slower result counts than simple plurality elections. The two major parties lose some structural advantages — the veto power of a separate runoff and, in some states, the gatekeeping of a closed primary — and could face races where their preferred candidate loses to a consensus second choice.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and state election offices

drawbacks.text: Ranked choice voting is harder to run: ballots are longer and easier to mismark, counting takes multiple rounds that can delay results, and the bill itself anticipates complexities like 'inactive ballots,' skipped or repeated rankings, and ties broken by lot [S2].

The federal grants are set at only $4–$8 per registered voter, and the underlying appropriation is authorized at 'such sums as may be necessary' with no fixed total, so states could be left covering costs if appropriations fall short [S2].

The bill overrides state election laws for federal elections under Congress's constitutional power over the 'time, place, and manner' of congressional elections, a broad federal preemption that state officials and courts may contest, even though it leaves state and local elections untouched [S2].

Voters who rank all their choices and see all of them eliminated, or who skip rankings, may have their ballots exhausted before the final round, meaning some votes never count in the deciding round — a fairness concern RCV states like Maine and Alaska have wrestled with [S2].

The private enforcement mechanism lets any state resident sue with fast-tracked three-judge-court review and no appeal except to the D.C. Circuit en banc, a streamlined process that could generate repeated litigation around every federal election cycle [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters, the core trade is favorable: more expressive ballots, no vote splitting, and majority winners, paid for with federal money rather than state budgets. The real costs are operational — slower counts, harder ballots, litigation risk — and there is a genuine question whether $4–$8 per registered voter is enough for a nationwide systems overhaul. The 2030 effective date and the exclusion of state and local races soften the transition. The main weakness is not design but power: the bill changes the rules of congressional elections, which is exactly why it has found no Republican cosponsors and no committee movement.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the House on December 10, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Administration Committee, which has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD) introduced the Ranked Choice Voting Act on December 10, 2025 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day, and the committee's action history shows no markup, hearing, or vote since [S4].
Sixteen House members — Raskin plus 15 cosponsors, all Democrats — are attached to the bill; no Republican has signed on [S3].
The bill would take effect only for federal elections held on or after January 1, 2030 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The two major parties keep the current election rules — plurality voting, separate runoffs, and state-controlled primaries — with no vote ever taken on ranked choice voting. Incumbent officeholders benefit from the status quo they were elected under.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The two major parties and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: Ranked choice voting weakens the parties' structural advantages: separate runoffs are banned, candidates cannot win by splitting a plurality, and party ballot access is measured from a candidate's best round rather than the final count. Both parties can benefit from runoff-free, no-spoil elections, but each loses the gatekeeping power of the current rules — which is why the bill has attracted support only from one party.

industries.industry: Election technology and voting equipment vendors
industries.note: The bill mandates equipment updates, new tabulation software, ballot redesign, and audits, and pays states $4–$8 per registered voter specifically for those systems, creating a large federally funded market for voting-system upgrades.

Because voters can rank a third-party candidate first without electing their least favorite, the vote-splitting penalty disappears, and ballot-access vote counts are calculated from the candidate's best round of tabulation.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support, no committee action three weeks after introduction, and a 2030 effective date, the bill is very likely to die in the House Administration Committee this Congress, as most voting-system overhaul bills from the minority party do. Its realistic function is to place a marker for future Congresses or for states to adopt ranked choice voting on their own.
